title: Ghosts in the Genome: Scientists Uncover Two Hidden Human Ancestors in Our DNA
summary: Imagine discovering a long-lost relative you never knew existed—not through old photos, but hidden inside your own genetic code. That's exactly what researchers at UC Berkeley have done, identifying two mysterious "ghost" ancestors that left their mark in the DNA of every living human. The findings, published July 30 in Science, add a startling new chapter to the story of human evolution. One of these ghost populations interbred with Homo sapiens in Africa more than 50,000 years ago, before the major migration out of the continent. Today, roughly 1% of the modern human genome comes from this lineage—comparable to the Neanderthal DNA many people carry. Strikingly, this ghost ancestry appears in all modern humans, not just those of African descent. "Previous publications suggested there might be ghost ancestry, but they hadn't concluded whether this unknown ancestry is present only in Africans or not," said Yulin Zhang, a Berkeley graduate student and co-first author. "We were able to find and map genomic locations in modern humans that are from this ghost lineage and show that this ghost ancestry is in all modern humans." The second discovery is even more ancient. A "super-archaic" ancestor, which split from our lineage about 1.8 million years ago, interbred with Denisovans in Eurasia over 200,000 years ago. When Denisovans later mixed with modern humans, a tiny fraction of that super-archaic DNA hitched a ride into our genomes. "The super-archaic finding is particularly exciting because it reveals genetic contributions from a human lineage that lived over a million years ago, despite the absence of any sequenced DNA from that population," said Arjun Biddanda, a postdoctoral researcher at Johns Hopkins and co-first author. The team developed a new computational method called TRACE (TRacking Archaic Contributions via ARG Estimation) that reconstructs ancient genealogical connections from hundreds of present-day genomes. This approach bypasses the need for fossil DNA, which is often unavailable. The results challenge the traditional view of human evolution as a simple branching tree. Instead, it resembles a complex web of populations connected by repeated migration and interbreeding. "We often think of human evolution as a branching tree, but new genomic data reveal a much more interconnected history," said senior author Priya Moorjani. The identities of these ghost populations remain unknown, but their estimated divergence times align with Middle Pleistocene Homo groups in Africa and Homo erectus in Eurasia. The study underscores how much of our deep past still lies hidden within us, waiting to be decoded.
why_it_matters: Our own DNA acts like a time capsule, carrying remnants of ancient human groups that disappeared long ago—revealing that human history is far more interconnected than textbooks once said, and that the story of our species is still being rewritten from within.

background_read: Denisovans (a group of ancient humans known only from a few bones and teeth found in a Siberian cave) and Neanderthals (stocky, large-brained hominins who lived in Europe and western Asia until about 40,000 years ago) are the best-known examples of extinct human cousins that interbred with our direct ancestors.

Scientists once pictured human evolution as a tidy branching tree, but DNA evidence has repeatedly revealed a tangled web of interbreeding among groups that split apart hundreds of thousands of years earlier.

The new study taps into this hidden history using a technique that rebuilds ancient family trees from modern genomes alone, without needing fossil DNA—a major advantage because DNA degrades over time and is rarely recoverable from very old remains.
Article_Structure: LEAD: A vivid metaphor—discovering a long-lost relative hidden in your own genetic code.
KEY FINDING 1: An African ghost population interbred with Homo sapiens over 50,000 years ago, contributing ~1% DNA to all living humans.
KEY FINDING 2: A 'super-archaic' ancestor that split 1.8 million years ago later interbred with Denisovans, leaving a tiny genetic trace in us.
EVIDENCE & METHOD: Quotes from researchers Yulin Zhang and Arjun Biddanda introduce the new TRACE computational method that bypasses fossil DNA.
BROADER IMPLICATION: Quote from senior author Priya Moorjani reframes human evolution as a complex web, not a simple tree.
OPEN QUESTION: The ghost populations' identities remain unknown, though their divergence times align with Middle Pleistocene Homo groups and Homo erectus.

perspectives.description: This discovery shows how powerful modern genomics can be: even without fossils, we can detect and map genetic contributions from ancestors who lived a million years ago. The new TRACE method may unlock many more hidden chapters of human evolution, helping us understand exactly how different human groups interacted.

Because the ghost populations are inferred entirely from DNA statistics, some researchers may remain cautious. Without physical fossils or archaeological evidence, it's hard to know what these ancient humans looked like, how they lived, or whether the genetic signal might actually come from a different, already-known group.

The study reinforces a broader shift in biology: the tree model of evolution is often too simple. Reticulate evolution, where lineages split and later merge through interbreeding, appears to be common—not just in humans but across many species. The Denisovan and Neanderthal gene flow into modern humans already showed this, and now the web extends even deeper.

Future work could try to tie the genetic ghost signals to specific fossil groups, like Homo erectus in Eurasia or a Middle Pleistocene population in Africa. The technique might also be applied to other species to reveal hidden hybridization events, and as more present-day genomes are sequenced, the resolution of these ancient relationships will only improve.
